posts.title: Race breakdown: Tarawera Ultra-Trail by UTMB 102K (single image)
posts.caption:
Tarawera Ultra-Trail by UTMB 102K is on Feb 13, 2027, and humidity is what sets it apart: mornings start near 97%, and in 2024 it reached 75°F (23.9°C) by 4 pm.

A typical high of 74°F (23.1°C) doesn't look hot on paper, but sticky air over 63.4 mi (102 km) and 7,546 ft (2,300 m) of climbing is a different race from a cool, dry long run. Race day is about 14 weeks out.

When to start, counted back from Feb 13:

✅ Gut: race fuel in long runs from Nov 21, race-level carbs by Jan 2 to Jan 16
✅ Hydration: sweat-rate weigh-ins across easy and hard runs now, then one in warm, humid weather about Jan 16 to 23
✅ Climbing: all block long, carried into the taper at lower volume

General guidelines, not a prescription. The hot-weather weigh-in timing is Raceproof's own, not from a study. Drink to a plan, never more than you sweat.

Full breakdown: raceproof.ai/races/tarawera-ultra-trail-102k (link in bio).

SOURCES: Race numbers and weather: Raceproof's Tarawera race page. Windows: Raceproof adaptation windows. Weigh-ins: Raceproof coach consensus (coaching practice); never drink more than you sweat: Hew-Butler et al. 2015.

posts.title: Pro breakdown: Vincent Luis, Kona 2026 (race breakdown variant)
posts.caption:
Vincent Luis won the 2026 IRONMAN World Championship in Kona in 7:47:27, and heat was the race's biggest demand: 88°F (31°C) at Kona airport, with humidity between 61% and 88% from 6 am to 5 pm.

In his own words, he prepared in stages. Hot baths and sauna in January and February. Easy rides and runs in the heat before IRONMAN Texas in April. Then, 3 weeks out, IRONMAN-pace sessions in a heat chamber at 90°F (32°C) and 80% humidity. On race day he says he took about 145 g of carbs an hour on the bike and about 100 g an hour on the run, "which is what we practiced in training", plus 54 to 57 oz (1.6 or 1.7 L) of fluid an hour on the bike.

Our take: copy the timing, not the numbers. Heat builds over 1 to 2 weeks and about 2.5% fades for every day without it. His 145 g/h is an elite, trained gut; guidelines go up to 90 g/h for races over 2.5 to 3 hours.

When to start, counted back from your race:

✅ Heat: build 6 to 2 weeks out, then 1 or 2 short sessions a week to race day
✅ Gut: race fuel in long sessions from 12 weeks out, race-level carbs by 4 to 6 weeks out

General guidelines, not a prescription. Heart condition, pregnancy or medication that affects heat tolerance? Talk to your doctor before heat sessions, hot baths or sauna.

Limits: n = 1, elite, one race. His numbers are self-reported in interviews; sodium and caffeine weren't released. The All-In Triathlon episode is sponsored by Precision Fuel & Hydration; his nutrition partner is 6d Sports Nutrition.

How many weeks out do you start heat work for a hot race?

Save this for your next build.

SOURCES: Official IRONMAN results. Weather: PHKO via Weather Underground; IRONMAN course page. His words: All-In Triathlon, ProTriNews, The Triathlon Hour. Tri247, Slowtwitch. Racinais 2015, Daanen 2018, Morton 2026 (Science in Sport ties), von Känel-Cordoba 2026, ADA/DC/ACSM 2016, Jiménez-Alfageme 2025. Raceproof adaptation windows. Concept via @sisu_endurancelab.

altText: Pro breakdown, Kona 2026. Vincent Luis won Kona on about 145 g of carbs an hour, after heat-chamber sessions at 90°F (32°C). 80% humidity in the chamber. 1st in 7:47:27. 2026 IRONMAN World Championship, Oct 10, 2026, n = 1.

The race, official results: sixth off the bike, winner by 1:35. Swim 48:31, bike 4:15:42, run 2:38:36, total 7:47:27. Out of T2 6:04 behind Ditlev, led from the mile 21 aid station, Gustav Iden 2nd in 7:49:02.

The course: heat and humidity all day. High at Kona airport 88°F (31°C). 6:53 am 79°F (26°C) at 88% humidity. Humidity 61 to 88% from 6 am to 5 pm. Average water 79°F (26°C). Heat, Hydration, Gut and Pacing all rated High.

What it took, our take: heat, repeated sessions over 1 to 2 weeks kept close to race day, about 2.5% fades per day without heat (Racinais 2015, Daanen 2018). Gut: a trained gut, experts put the ceiling near 120 g/h for trained athletes (Morton 2026). Pacing: conservative 70.3 bike pacing was linked to a better run (von Känel-Cordoba 2026). Our take, not measured.

What we know he did, his words: January to February, hot baths and sauna. Before Texas in April, easy rides and runs in the heat. 3 weeks out, IRONMAN-pace sessions in a heat chamber at 90°F (32°C), 80% humidity. Race day: about 145 g/h on the bike, about 100 g/h on the run, 54 to 57 oz (1.6 or 1.7 L) of fluid an hour on the bike. Self-reported; sodium and caffeine not released.
You vs the pro, our take: Luis on the bike about 145 g/h, guideline up to 90 g/h for races over 2.5 to 3 hours, Seville marathoners average 35 g/h.

Test it yourself: copy the timing, not the numbers. Build heat sessions 6 to 2 weeks out, then 1 or 2 short ones a week to race day. Build up gradually; talk to your doctor first with a heart condition, pregnancy or medication that affects heat tolerance. Raceproof checks: Heat.

Sources and credits: official IRONMAN results, PHKO weather via Weather Underground, IRONMAN course page, interviews on All-In Triathlon (sponsored by Precision Fuel & Hydration), ProTriNews and The Triathlon Hour, Tri247, Slowtwitch, and the studies cited. n = 1, self-reported. Nutrition partner 6d Sports Nutrition. Concept via @sisu_endurancelab.

posts.title: Stats recap: Races are lost in training (Backup item, triathlon Reel slot)
posts.caption:
Races are lost in training. Four numbers that show it:

28% of men and 17% of women hit the wall in a marathon, losing about 30 minutes on average.

96% of runners at a 100-mile race had at least one stomach symptom, most of them mild. GI issues contributed to 36% of DNFs.

30% of 2,407 UTMB 2026 starters didn't finish, citing fatigue, digestive problems and falling behind on food.

In the hottest marathons, top men ran 4.5% off course records, against 1.7% in the coolest: about 2.6 times more time lost. Slower runners lost more.

Each one has a warning sign in training, weeks before race day: race fuel never practiced on long runs, goal pace never held on tired legs, no heat work for a hot race. Raceproof checks your training against what your race will demand, while there's still time to fix it. Keep your coach. Keep your plan. Coming spring 2027.

Join the waitlist. Link in bio. Share with a training partner: 3 friends get you a free race pass.

SOURCES: The wall: Smyth 2021, PLOS ONE. 100-mile stomach symptoms: Stuempfle & Hoffman 2015, Journal of Sports Sciences. UTMB 2026: Reference Trail. Heat: Ely et al. 2007, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise.

posts.title: Product: what Raceproof checks, Heat and Hydration close-up (Backup item, marathon carousel slot)
posts.caption:
Racing somewhere hot? Two pillars decide most of it: heat and hydration. Here's how Raceproof checks both.

Heat is automatic. Raceproof compares the sessions you've trained in heat with your race forecast, for races with a typical high of 80°F (27°C) or more. Heat builds in about 10 to 14 days of regular sessions and fades within a few weeks without them.

Hydration takes a quick log. Weigh in before and after a few sessions, or enter an hDrop or lab sweat test, and Raceproof tracks your sweat rate against your race plan. Coaches use 3 or more weigh-ins across easy and hard sessions and different temperatures. Those numbers come from coaches, not studies. Then drink to a plan, never more than you sweat.

When to start, counted back from your race:

✅ Hydration: first weigh-ins 16 to 12 weeks out; for a hot race, one in race-like heat 4 to 3 weeks out
✅ Heat: build 6 to 2 weeks out, then 1 or 2 short sessions a week to race day

General guidelines, not a prescription. Heart condition, pregnancy or medication that affects heat tolerance? Talk to your doctor before heat sessions.

Raceproof never writes or changes your plan. Coming spring 2027. Join the waitlist. Link in bio.

SOURCES: Heat windows: Raceproof adaptation windows (Racinais 2015, Tyler 2016, Daanen 2018, Périard 2015). Weigh-in count and timing: Raceproof coach consensus (coaching practice). Overdrinking: Hew-Butler et al. 2015, Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine.

posts.title: Pain: Durability, your legs quit late
posts.caption:
Your legs quit late. Your long runs never tested goal pace on tired legs.

If your long runs are always easy and your goal-pace work is always fresh, race day is the first time you hold goal pace on tired legs.

The fix: run long every 1 to 2 weeks, with your longest runs 8 to 4 weeks out, and in the last 10 weeks finish some of those runs at goal pace. That timing comes from coaches, not studies. In one study, runners who regularly ran 90 minutes or more lost less running economy late in a 90-minute threshold run than runners whose runs stayed under 70 minutes (3.1% vs 6.0%): a link, not proof. New to long runs? Keep each one within about 10% of your longest in the past 30 days.

General guidelines, not a prescription.

Raceproof checks durability every week, alongside the plan you already follow. Coming spring 2027. Join the waitlist. Link in bio.

SOURCES: Long-run timing: Raceproof coach consensus (Roche, Friel, McCrann, Sayer and 7 more coaches; coaching practice). Goal-pace window: Raceproof adaptation windows. Late-run economy: Zanini et al. 2026, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 10% cap: Frandsen et al. 2025, British Journal of Sports Medicine.

reels.title: Research blog Reel: Your finish time sets your carb target (Backup item, Thursday blog slot)
reels.caption:
Your finish time sets your carb target. Most marathoners take far less.

Guidelines put a 2 to 3 hour effort at about 60 g of carbs an hour, and races longer than about 2.5 to 3 hours at up to 90 g/h. At the 2022 Seville Marathon, 160 runners averaged 35 g/h, and only 9% reached 60 to 90 g/h. That's self-reported intake at one race: a link, not proof.

Your gut can be trained to take more, but it needs weeks, not a race-week fix.

When to start, counted back from your race:

✅ Gut: race fuel in long runs from 12 to 8 weeks out, race-level carbs by 4 to 6 weeks out

General guidelines, not a prescription.

How many g/h do you take in a marathon?

Full article: raceproof.ai/blog/carbs-per-hour-marathon (link in bio).

SOURCES: Guidelines: ADA, DC and ACSM 2016. Seville intake: Jiménez-Alfageme et al. 2025, Sports Medicine Open. Gut window: Raceproof adaptation windows.

reels.caption:
I have two coaches, and I still built Raceproof.

My coaches write my training. Raceproof checks whether that training covers what my race will ask: gut, hydration, heat, terrain, durability, pacing and taper. It never writes or changes the plan. Link your coach once, and your readiness reports reach them after every training session.

Keep your coach. Keep your plan. Coming spring 2027.
